clue.text: Nearly steal original version, after book comes out

indicators.note: after means the trimmed steal and the manuscript follow the book's letter
nearly means the word is cut short by its final letter

parts.note: to steal is to loot
MS, a manuscript, is the original version of a text

explanation.surface: A thief nearly makes off with an original manuscript once a book has been published.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nearly' trims LOOT to LOO. 'Comes out' looks like part of the book's publication, but it is the definition, as flowers do.
explanation.definitionFit: A flower blooms when it opens, so a plant that comes out into flower is said to bloom.

clue.text: Like some housing support? Go here, joining queue

parts.note: to back means to support
joining a queue you go to the back

explanation.surface: Someone asks about support for housing and is told to join the end of a line.
explanation.walkthrough: Back-to-back houses are British terraced houses built sharing a rear wall, typical of industrial towns.
explanation.definitionFit: Back-to-back houses are built in rows joined at the rear wall, a style of British terraced housing.

clue.text: Mollusc, once having been separated from female

indicators.note: separated from means the letter is removed from the word

parts.note: former means having once been

explanation.surface: A shellfish that used to be with its mate has been parted from her.
explanation.definitionFit: An ormer is an abalone, an edible sea snail found off the Channel Islands.

clue.text: Church decorated with jolly expensive fabrics

indicators.note: decorated with means the first word is set within the other, as an ornament

parts.note: merry means jolly
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A church is adorned with very costly cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jolly' looks like the British intensifier meaning very; it is merry.
explanation.definitionFit: Mercery is the stock of a mercer, a dealer in fine fabrics such as silks and velvets.

clue.text: Time for larks in very short holiday

definitions.meaning: larks are early risers and singers at first light, so their time is the dawn
a break from work lasting just one day

explanation.surface: Early risers enjoy themselves during a quick day off.
explanation.definitionFit: Dawn is when larks sing, and a one-day holiday is literally a day's break; both senses fit.

clue.text: Extra bill teacher submitted

indicators.note: submitted means placed below, as this is a down clue

parts.note: a bill is an advertisement, an ad
a don is a university teacher

explanation.surface: A teacher has submitted an additional bill.
explanation.definitionFit: An add-on is an extra item attached to something, such as an optional extra.

clue.text: Club bowler covers miles; this to absorb the drips?

parts.note: a bat is a club

indicators.note: covers means the hat goes round the letter

parts.note: a bowler is a hat

explanation.surface: A cricket club's bowler covers many miles, so needs something to soak up sweat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Club bowler' suggests a cricketer; a bowler is a hat and a club a bat.
explanation.definitionFit: A bath mat soaks up the water that drips off someone climbing out of the bath.

clue.text: In places I corrected work of bencher

indicators.note: in means the work goes inside the rearranged letters
corrected means the letters are put into a new order

parts.note: op, opus, means a work

explanation.surface: A lawyer's work in court has been corrected in places.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corrected' reshuffles the letters of places and I, and 'In' puts the work inside them. A bencher seems a lawyer, but bishops sit on the bishops' bench in the House of Lords.
explanation.definitionFit: Episcopal means relating to bishops, who sit on the bench of bishops in the House of Lords.

clue.text: Writing up approval, and confirmation, for executioner

indicators.note: writing up means reading upwards in a down clue, so both words are turned

parts.note: OK signals approval
OK is a confirmation

explanation.surface: Someone records consent and confirmation for an execution.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Writing up' turns each OK into KO in place.
explanation.definitionFit: Ko-Ko is the Lord High Executioner in Gilbert and Sullivan's operetta The Mikado.

clue.text: Capital man to christen ship

parts.note: to dub is to name or christen
a liner is a ship

explanation.surface: An important man is chosen to name a ship at its launch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital man' looks like a top fellow; it is a man from a capital, Dublin.
explanation.definitionFit: A Dubliner is a native of Dublin, the capital city of Ireland.

clue.text: Finally agree to call

definitions.meaning: to be persuaded at last to accept a view
to call on someone is to pay them a visit

explanation.surface: Someone at last consents to make a phone call.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both to be won over in the end and to visit someone's home.

clue.text: Skilful feat made with finesse, perhaps

definitions.meaning: a clever stunt such as a conjuror performs
in bridge a finesse is a play that can win a round of cards

explanation.surface: A clever stunt carried off with delicate skill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finesse' looks like general delicacy, but in the card game bridge it is a technical play for winning a round.
explanation.definitionFit: A deft stunt is a trick, and in bridge each round of cards won is called a trick.

clue.text: Detailed results for these runners

parts.note: read 'detailed' as de-tailed: the runners of the nursery rhyme had their tails cut off by the farmer's wife

explanation.surface: Full results are published for a group of race entrants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Detailed' seems to mean thorough; read it as tails removed. The nursery rhyme's refrain is 'see how they run', hence runners.
explanation.definitionFit: In the nursery rhyme three sightless rodents run after the farmer's wife, who cuts off their tails with a carving knife.

clue.text: Unsociable guy goes to party

parts.note: a guy is a rope used as a stay
an at-home is a party held in one's house

explanation.surface: An unfriendly man goes off to a social event.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guy' looks like a man; it is a guy rope, a stay.
explanation.definitionFit: A stay-at-home person avoids going out, so is unsociable.

clue.text: Twist past, holding a small volume

indicators.note: holding means the first piece wraps round the others

parts.note: by can mean past, as in 'walk by'
cc, cubic centimetres, measures a small volume

explanation.surface: Someone twists past a container holding a little liquid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twist' is a twist of tobacco, a small rolled quantity, and BACCY is a British slang word for tobacco.
explanation.definitionFit: Tobacco was sold as a twist, a rolled plug, and baccy is the colloquial word for tobacco.

clue.text: Ordered us to clean office

indicators.note: ordered means the letters are rearranged into a new sequence

explanation.surface: A boss tells staff to clean the office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ordered' rearranges USTOCLEAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A consulate is the office of a consul representing a foreign country.

clue.text: Everything bet on something black — spades or a club

indicators.note: on means the stake is placed after the colour and the suit in this across answer

parts.note: night is the black part of the day
S is the card-game abbreviation for spades
the pot is all the money staked in a hand

explanation.surface: A gambler stakes everything on a black colour at roulette, or at cards on spades or clubs.
explanation.walkthrough: The gambling words suggest roulette and cards; 'a club' turns out to be a nightclub, the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A nightspot is a nightclub or late-opening entertainment venue, so it is a kind of club.

clue.text: Hard to succeed, after team ran off, he noted

indicators.note: after means hard and succeed follow the shortened team
off means the letters are taken away from the team's name

parts.note: Rangers is a Glasgow football team
these letters are removed as written
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils
to win is to succeed

explanation.surface: It's hard to win once the team has fled, he remarked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ran off' takes RAN from RANGERS, a Scottish football club, leaving GERS. 'He noted' means a writer of music notes.
explanation.definitionFit: George Gershwin was an American composer, a man who wrote down musical notes.

clue.text: For one, William's against disheartening strange men

parts.note: con means against, as in pros and cons

indicators.note: disheartening means the word loses its central letter

parts.note: queer means strange or odd
OR, other ranks, means ordinary soldiers, men

explanation.surface: William is said to oppose the dispiriting of some odd men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disheartening' takes the middle E out of QUEER, leaving QUER. William I of England was called William the Conqueror.
explanation.definitionFit: William I is known by the title of Conqueror, so the title is William's, for one example.

clue.text: Wily chap's sly moves contributing to advantages

indicators.note: contributing to means the shuffled letters are put inside the other word

parts.note: uses are benefits, advantages

indicators.note: moves means the letters are shifted about

explanation.surface: A crafty man's cunning moves add to his gains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moves' reshuffles sly, which 'contributing to' places inside the advantages. Ulysses is the Roman name of wily Odysseus.
explanation.definitionFit: Ulysses, the Latin Odysseus, is famous in Homer for his cunning, notably the wooden horse.

clue.text: Hubby finally posted to Flanders? Yes, she kept saying

indicators.note: posted to means the following letter is attached after the name

parts.note: Moll Flanders is the heroine of Defoe's novel

indicators.note: finally means the last letter of the word is taken

explanation.surface: A wartime wife agrees to send her husband's mail to the Flanders front.
explanation.walkthrough: Flanders looks like the First World War battlefield but is Defoe's heroine Moll. Molly Bloom in Joyce's Ulysses ends her soliloquy repeating 'yes'.
explanation.definitionFit: Molly Bloom's closing monologue in Joyce's novel repeats 'yes' throughout and ends on it.

clue.text: Artist has to mark a paper not acceptable

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for mark, the old German currency

indicators.note: not acceptable means losing U, the letter for upper-class acceptability

parts.note: tissue is a thin paper

explanation.surface: An artist must mark a paper that is unacceptable.
explanation.walkthrough: U stands for upper-class, hence socially acceptable; 'not acceptable' removes it from TISSUE.
explanation.definitionFit: Henri Matisse was a French painter, leading figure of the Fauvist movement.

clue.text: Settle quarrel over sinking of cutter

definitions.meaning: to make peace and end a feud
literally sinking an axe, a cutting tool, into the ground

explanation.surface: A dispute is settled about the loss of a small sailing ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cutter' suggests the sailing vessel, and 'sinking' the loss at sea; it is the axe, sunk into earth.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for making peace comes from the custom of burying a war axe as a sign of truce.

clue.text: Pig gets an earth-covered hut

parts.note: a hog is a pig

explanation.surface: A pig is given a small mud shelter to live in.
explanation.definitionFit: A hogan is a traditional Navajo dwelling built of logs and covered with earth.

clue.text: Beauty aid woman finds inapplicable

parts.note: hen is slang for a woman
NA, not applicable, means inapplicable

explanation.surface: A woman decides a cosmetic doesn't suit her.
explanation.definitionFit: Henna is a reddish plant dye used as a cosmetic for colouring hair and skin.

clue.text: Be roused by late party

definitions.meaning: a gathering held after a death to honour the late person

explanation.surface: Someone is woken by a party that runs late.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Late party' suggests a party running into the night; it is a gathering for the late, the dead.
explanation.definitionFit: To come out of sleep is to wake, and a wake is the watch or gathering held after a death.

clue.text: Collect admission of stupidity?

definitions.meaning: a person confessing 'I am an ass', shortened to two words

explanation.surface: Someone owns up to being foolish when asked to gather things.
explanation.definitionFit: To accumulate is to collect, and split as 'am ass' it is someone owning that they are a fool.

clue.text: See lad sing so badly, with undistinguished tones …

indicators.note: badly signals that the letters are put in a disordered arrangement

explanation.surface: Watch the boy sing poorly, with his notes all blurred together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' is a link word. 'Badly' reshuffles LADSINGSO.
explanation.definitionFit: In music, a glissando slides through notes so that individual pitches are not separately distinguished.

clue.text: … prayers, nevertheless, useless

parts.note: even so means nevertheless
NG, no good, means useless

explanation.surface: Prayers are offered, though to no effect.
explanation.definitionFit: Evening prayer in the Anglican church service is called evensong.

clue.text: People have to get on -—- they live together

parts.note: men means people
to get on in years is to age

explanation.surface: People need to get along if they share a house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get on' suggests getting along together; it means growing older.
explanation.definitionFit: A menage is a household, the people who live together under one roof.
